notes.note: Angular 22's CLI hard-refuses Node 24.13 (needs ^22.22.3 || ^24.15 || >=26) with an error that names the requirement but not the fix. A cold start on a slightly stale Node loses several minutes here. The root package.json now declares `engines`, but pnpm only warns; consider `engine-strict` if this bites again.

pnpm 11 fails `pnpm install` outright with ERR_PNPM_IGNORED_BUILDS rather than warning, and rewrites pnpm-workspace.yaml with `allowBuilds` placeholders that must be edited by hand. Anyone cloning this repo will hit it once. Worth a line in the README if a second person ever sets this up.

Two review rounds on the plan and one on the diff each found a real defect that the previous round had introduced or missed — most sharply, the shutdown test was vacuous twice in a row for two different reasons. Verifying a test by mutation (delete the line it claims to cover, watch it fail) took about a minute and was the only thing that actually settled it. Worth doing routinely for tests that guard a failure path.

A `tsx watch` from an earlier session outlived its parent and kept port 4310, so the next `pnpm dev` printed the EADDRINUSE message and the host died while `ng serve` carried on. The error path did its job — the message named the port and the cause — but on Windows an orphaned watcher is easy to leave behind and the symptom (web up, host silently absent) is confusing. If this recurs, `netstat -ano | findstr :4310` then Stop-Process is the fix.

`pnpm -r` interleaves and prefixes output, so a truncated view of `pnpm test` can look like only one workspace ran. Cost a few minutes of false alarm. Not worth fixing; worth remembering when reading CI logs.

Packages-as-source has a resolution tax that only shows up at the consumer. `pnpm --filter @cwm/contracts test` and every tsc pass were green while `apps/web`'s vitest run failed to resolve `zod` — the Angular builder inlines the contracts source into the app's own module graph, so the transitive dependency has to be a direct dependency of `apps/web`. Expect the same for every future package dependency, and check the web suite, not just the package's own.

The real JsonDataStore exercise could verify a realistic document, a two-repository unit of work, atomic replacement, and reload, but not the actual host/UI path: Slice 4 owns the first reusable seeds and Slice 5 owns host wiring. That boundary makes Slice 3's §77 hands-on check necessarily storage-level; the temporary scenario reloaded two projects and a completed task successfully, with no leftover temp file.

Building the first real section fixtures exposed that `SectionColumnSpanSchema = z.literal([12, 8, 6, 4])` is a Zod overload for the union 12|8|6|4, not an array-shaped column span. The schema is correct and the seed failure was useful, but the declaration is visually misleading enough to re-check before writing future section literals.

Driving the API by hand found what 93 passing tests did not: every timestamp in a host session was identical. PrototypeClock is settable-and-frozen, which is exactly right for a test and exactly wrong for a running host — a task's createdAt, completedAt and archivedAt all matched to the millisecond, and the §57 feed was one undifferentiated tie. Added SimulatedClock (real time plus a settable offset) for the host and left PrototypeClock to the tests. AGENTS §3 Step 4 earned its place here; no amount of unit testing would have surfaced this, because the tests *want* a frozen clock.

The concurrency test was vacuously green for a day. Five simultaneous POSTs against an in-memory store never actually overlap — persist() finishes inside one task, so the next request's unit of work starts cleanly and a naive non-serializing adapter passes. Only rewriting it over a real JsonDataStore (where file I/O keeps a unit open across ticks) made it fail without serialization. Mutation testing is what caught it: breaking unitOfWorkFor on purpose and watching the suite stay green. That trick has now caught something in two consecutive slices.

`node --import tsx apps/prototype-host/main.ts` from the repo root fails with ERR_MODULE_NOT_FOUND for tsx: pnpm's isolated node_modules only links it inside apps/prototype-host, so the loader has to be resolved with that as cwd. Cost a few confused minutes. scripts/acceptance.mjs sets `cwd: hostRoot` for this reason — worth remembering before Slice 15 spawns an MCP stdio process the same way.

The seeds are built around SEED_NOW (2026-08-24) but the host clock starts at real time, so the moment you add a task to `busy-week` it sits days after every seeded due date and `overdue-chaos` stops reading as overdue. SimulatedClock.setNow is the mechanism; Slice 12's dev panel is where the control belongs. Until then a seed's scenario decays a little more each day, which will quietly mislead anyone evaluating the dashboard (§24) or calendar (§37). Worth deciding in Slice 12 whether loading a seed should also set the clock to that seed's SEED_NOW.

Two rounds of plan review found the same file twice, for different reasons: unitOfWorkFor. Round 1 caught that a pass-through adapter 500s on any two interleaved requests; round 2 caught that the queue fixing that would deadlock on a nested call. Both were real. The thing that settled it was not a third review but a 40-line spike run against the actual InMemoryDataStore — nested join, overlap, and failure recovery, printed. Reviewing an async-context design on paper is much worse value than running it.

The scariest bug of the slice was found by a review agent and confirmed by accident: an unguarded ancestor walk over an already-cyclic document does not hang one request, it starves the event loop and wedges the whole process — timers stop, the server stops answering, Ctrl+C's handler never runs. I discovered this by writing the test for it, which hung the test runner for three minutes with a 1s Promise.race that never fired. Any await-in-a-loop over synchronously-resolving repository reads has this shape. Worth remembering before Slice 20 walks subtask trees and Slice 11 walks projects for the dashboard.

Two guards written a day apart disagreed about the same problem. ProjectService carries an explicit comment — 'the exposed route is PATCH, so a rule only archive() enforced would be decorative' — and TaskService then shipped exactly that bug: complete() refused an archived task, PATCH {status:'done'} did not. Knowing the trap and writing the comment was not enough to avoid it in the next file. A rule that has two entry points needs a test per entry point, not a note.

The custom lint I wrote to enforce §12 was mostly theatre: it walked only top-level import declarations, so `export { JsonDataStore } from '@cwm/repositories'` in index.ts — plus a clean relative import from every sibling — sailed through, as did import(), require(), and `fs/promises` against a ban list that named `fs`. A ban list cannot survive the next dependency; it is now an allowlist over a full tree walk. Writing the six self-tests then found two bugs in the rewrite. A lint without a test that it FAILS on each violation form is a lint you are guessing about.

Running the shell with the host stopped surfaced a boundary hole the whole test suite had missed: the sidebar rendered 'Failed to fetch'. The gateway maps every transport failure to a GatewayError, but PrototypeIdentityProvider did not — and since every gateway call awaits getCurrentIdentity() first, the identity provider is the failure the user actually meets. §8's rule reads 'components depend on gateway interfaces', so I built the mapping in one of the two boundary classes and not the other. The tests all passed because each one mocked the layer under test. Only running it found this.

The host obeys a bare PORT environment variable, so any tool that sets PORT=4200 to launch the web app takes :4310 away from the host — and because concurrently starts both, the host wins the bind and Angular quietly moves elsewhere. What the browser then shows at :4200 is {"error":"not_found"} in the host's own words, which reads like a routing bug in the app. A shared, extremely common variable name is the wrong knob for one of two processes in a single `pnpm dev`.

`pnpm prototype:seed nested-projects` while the app is running changes nothing on screen and gives no hint why: the host reads data.json once at startup and holds it. I spent a confused minute assuming the sidebar was caching. §76's reset is going to need to be reachable from inside the app (Slice 12's dev panel) rather than only from a second terminal — or the host needs to notice the file changed.

With the host down the shell still renders — nav, theme, layout — and only the project list carries the error. That is the right shape, and it was worth having the sidebar take `error` as an input rather than owning a store: the failure had somewhere obvious to land. The top bar shows no persona at all in that state, which looks broken rather than degraded. Whether an unreachable host should be a shell-level banner instead of a sidebar line is a question for Slice 7, when a failed write needs somewhere to say so too (§63).

I wrote note-008 last slice — 'a lint without a test that it FAILS on each violation form is a lint you are guessing about' — and then shipped exactly that lint again. The token checker passed a probe file containing eleven deliberate literals: a component defining its own --my-accent palette, the first declaration after a nested Sass block, every non-px unit, oklch()/lab(), single-quoted style attributes, Angular [style.x] and [ngStyle] bindings, and any styles string containing a ${}. Two violations were already live in shipped code. The self-test was real but its fixtures were all single-line rules, which is the one shape where the bugs cancel out. Knowing the lesson and writing it down did not transfer; what would have caught it is writing the adversarial probe BEFORE believing the checker, not after review asked.

Hardening the checker immediately produced three false positives — content: "hex #fff means white", fill: url(#face), and font-family: Gold, Tan, Sienna — and my fix for those silently broke Angular binding detection, because a bound style value IS a quoted string and I had just started stripping quoted strings. Every tightening pass loosened something else. The only reason I caught it was keeping the original probe file and re-running it after each change. A lint needs two fixture sets that both run every time: the things it must catch, and the things it must not.

Review found the gateway turning 'match nothing' into 'match everything': list({status: []}) serialized to no query parameter, the host read that as no filter, and every project came back — the exact inverse of the request, and the opposite of what the same query does in-process. An adapter that is supposed to be a transparent transport for a query type has to answer for the values that do not survive the wire, and an empty array is the obvious one. Worth checking every other filter shape for the same class of thing when Slice 7 starts sending real TaskQuery values.

Two boundary classes, written an hour apart, disagreed about the same job: the gateway read the host's {error, message} envelope, and the identity provider mapped every status to internal_error and threw the message away. Same shape as Slice 5's ProjectService/TaskService archive-guard divergence (note-007). The pattern is now clear enough to name: whenever a rule or a translation has two entry points, the second one gets a worse version of it. The fix is not vigilance, it is one function both call — toGatewayError now lives in gateway-error.ts.

The first real-browser create found a contract/UI disagreement all component tests had missed: the host returned the new task with medium priority, but the detail drawer's native select visibly chose low. Angular applied the select value before the dynamic options existed, so the browser kept the first option. Adding an assertion for the selected control value failed exactly the same way in jsdom; explicit option selection fixed both. A select test that only fires change events proves writes, not what the user initially sees.

The temporary /tasks workspace is intentionally not linked from the shell, so the feature is undiscoverable without knowing its URL. That is acceptable for Slice 7's exercise route, but it makes the transition in Slice 8 load-bearing: project Task List sections must replace this route's discoverability rather than merely duplicate its behavior. Do not preserve /tasks as a second permanent task surface by inertia.

A project with one unfinished task showed "Not available" instead of "0%". The store was right; the template was `@if (store.progress(); as progress)`, and 0 is falsy, so a real zero took the no-value branch. Every unit test passed — they asserted the store, and the empty case, but never rendered a project where work simply had not started. Falsy-zero is worth checking by hand in any template that renders a count.

Duplicating a Task List section gives two frames listing the same tasks, each with its own quick-create, both writing to the same project. Nothing is broken — but §31 gives every section a duplicate control, and for a section backed by shared data it is not obvious what duplicating means. Duplicate is clearly useful for Rich Text. Worth asking in Slice 9 whether it belongs on every section type or only on ones that own their content.

Remove deletes a section immediately, with no confirmation and no undo. That was the right call for a prototype (§31 offers no undo, and a section is view configuration), but removing the Rich Text section also removes text someone wrote — the one section whose content lives in the section itself. If a real user ever loses a paragraph this way, the answer is probably a confirm on sections whose config is non-empty, not a general undo.

The preview runner sets PORT=4200 for `pnpm dev`, and `concurrently` passes it to both children — so the host read it too and took 4200 before ng serve could, leaving the web app answering {"error":"not_found"}. The host's PORT override is deliberate (it lets the acceptance script run a second host), so the fix is not to remove it. If this recurs, run `pnpm dev:web` and `pnpm dev:host` separately, or give the host its own variable name.
